routes.description: Establish that Bignon's experience, providentially interpreted coincidences, and supporting intellectual and historical considerations can jointly provide rational support for specifically Christian belief without compelling every observer.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the experiential pattern is rationally relevant under a comparative explanation, rival experiences do not neutralize it, and independent considerations can support its Christian interpretation at the modest standard of personal rational justification.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conversion experience and supporting considerations jointly make Christian belief rationally supportable despite naturalist and rival-religion alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Explain why the personally salient convergence of experiences and coincidences is more expected under providence than under an unaided naturalistic account.
Connect experience with intellectual considerations so the case supplies rational justification without requiring coercive or universally compelling proof.
Provide a principled way to distinguish the Christian interpretation from incompatible religious experiences through comparative intellectual and historical considerations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for why providential guidance in one conversion need not imply equivalent guidance or conversion opportunities for every person.
Clarify how surviving early Christian materials can aid access to historical claims without treating their abundance alone as proof of those claims.

routes.description: Establish that reverse conversions, culturally variable experiences, ordinary coincidence, and competing intellectual considerations remove any distinctive evidential advantage claimed for Bignon's Christian interpretation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic explanations adequately predict conversion patterns, rival experiences resist a uniquely Christian reading, and the proposed intellectual or historical adjudicators do not restore a clear evidential advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that rival experiences and naturalistic explanations undercut the claimed evidential force of Bignon's experience for specifically Christian belief.

centralBridges.description: Explain how large populations, ordinary coincidence, and culturally familiar narratives can generate apparently coordinated conversion stories without providential causation.
Show how culturally diverse and directionally opposed religious experiences weaken an inference from personal experience to Christianity in particular.
Establish that philosophical and historical considerations remain contested and do not plainly break the symmetry between Christian, rival-religious, and naturalist interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether selective providential intervention fits the persistence of reasonable nonbelief and the uneven distribution of conversion experiences.
Distinguish evidential quality from documentary quantity by considering how institutional dominance and preservation affect the surviving record.

sections.title: Providential pattern or natural coincidence
sections.rationale: This section addresses the primary explanatory clash over whether the conversion story's coordinated and personally salient events favor divine providence or are expected among many lives shaped by ordinary coincidence and familiar narratives.

sections.title: Personal justification and the cumulative case
sections.rationale: This section fixes the relevant epistemic burden and examines how experience, philosophical argument, and background considerations may combine to support belief without forcing rational convergence or excluding reasonable disagreement.

sections.title: Rival religious experiences and Christian specificity
sections.rationale: This section tests whether culturally diverse experiences, reverse conversions, and disputed exceptions neutralize specifically Christian support, or whether different experiences can be compared without dismissing all experiential evidence.

sections.title: Historical and intellectual adjudication
sections.rationale: This section considers whether historical sources and broader intellectual arguments can adjudicate between Christianity and rival interpretations when experiential claims appear balanced, including the significance and limits of the surviving documentary record.

sections.title: Selective providence and persistent nonbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether a providential account of one person's conversion can accommodate uneven divine guidance, persistent reasonable nonbelief, and competing considerations concerning hiddenness without undermining the proposed explanation.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: After intellectual barriers weakened, Bignon's experience of guilt made Christian atonement intelligible and led to trust in Christ, relief from guilt, and perceived spiritual rebirth.
moves.attributionBasis: Bignon explicitly confirms the host's characterization and then gives a continuous first-person explanation of the experience and its religious interpretation.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the experiential and atonement component of the cumulative epistemic route, connecting guilt, trust, relief, and perceived rebirth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops a material experiential component, though not the comparative warrant against rival explanations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The first-person sequence and the status of rebirth as an experienced interpretation are readily recoverable and consistently framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Certainty concerns the speaker's own experience and resulting trust, rather than a universal inference compelling outsiders.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experiential progression is internally consistent, with only the interpretation of relief as spiritual rebirth remaining inferentially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific first-person details support the autobiographical claim, but they do not independently verify the Christian causal interpretation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies an important experiential element of the central cumulative-epistemology bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move narrates and interprets a personal experience without engaging a meaningful live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt specifically links Christian atonement, trust in Jesus, evaporating guilt, and an experienced spiritual rebirth.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Conversion narratives run in opposing directions and can accompany reported improvements in values and meaning, so their existence alone supplies little net evidence for Christianity.
moves.attributionBasis: The host invites Oppy's assessment, and Oppy answers continuously by comparing familiar conversion patterns with stories of departure from Christianity.

components.text: Whether the narrated conversion and beneficial transformation provide distinctive support for Christianity rather than a direction-neutral conversion pattern.

response.rationale: Oppy directly contacts the evidential significance of the conversion story by adducing structurally similar narratives running away from Christianity and drawing a symmetry consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly challenges the decisive inference from conversion narrative to specifically Christian evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to the evidential value of stories existing in both directions, not their sincerity or all possible evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy cautiously says symmetry makes the net evidential value unclear and expressly avoids discrediting either group.

charity.alternative: A conversion story may include features beyond the bare fact of changing belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: The symmetry objection concerns the story's existence alone, not every detailed feature of Bignon's case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The symmetry inference is explicit and valid at its stated limited scope: opposing narratives reduce evidential force from narrative existence alone.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The familiar existence of reverse-conversion stories supports the comparison, though no representative prevalence evidence is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the indispensable rival-adjudication bridge by identifying directionally opposed experiential testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy preserves this decisive qualification and does not claim that reverse conversions refute every feature of the Christian case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly identifies stories running away from Christianity and concludes that stories in both directions complicate their total evidential value.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Although a change of belief is weak evidence by itself, the coordinated and personally significant improbabilities in Bignon's story are more expected if Christianity is true than if atheism is true.
moves.attributionBasis: Bignon resumes in the first person after Oppy's challenge and explicitly distinguishes bare conversion testimony from the particular features of his own account.

components.text: Whether Bignon relies merely on conversion testimony or on particular coordinated events whose likelihood differs between Christianity and atheism.

response.rationale: Bignon grants that bare conversion is weak and answers the symmetry challenge by shifting to identified coincidences and an explicitly comparative likelihood claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts and narrows the decisive symmetry premise, then supplies the alternative feature on which the evidential claim depends.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition and examples are clear, but the relevant probability space and meaning of expected remain under-specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is appropriately qualified, though the asserted likelihood advantage exceeds the undeveloped probability model supplied.

charity.alternative: Reverse conversions may neutralize evidence supplied merely by a person's change of belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon concedes that limited point and claims evidential weight only for the particular coordinated features of his story.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood comparison is coherent, but it leaves implicit why Christianity predicts these particular events better than atheism does.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete coincidences are named, yet their base rates, independence, and comparative likelihoods are not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central naturalistic-coincidence bridge at the point of comparative explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately accepts the strongest limited symmetry objection and isolates the precise residual issue requiring comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies hitchhiking, hotel-location, and church-exit events and expressly compares their expectation under Christianity and atheism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Across billions of lives, culturally familiar conversion scripts and ordinary coincidences can naturally generate apparently coordinated conversion stories without supernatural causation.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy takes the floor after Bignon's probabilistic claim, offers a counterexample, and then directly addresses the interpretation of the alleged improbabilities.

components.text: Whether the allegedly improbable coordinated events are less expected under naturalism once population size, familiar scripts, and ordinary coincidence are considered.

response.rationale: Oppy directly offers the missing naturalistic comparator: familiar cultural scripts operating over many people and accumulating ordinary coincidences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply squarely contacts the comparative-expectation premise and supplies a recognizable population-and-selection alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic mechanism is clear, with only an implicit limitation that it renders such stories unsurprising rather than proving every detail ordinary.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances a modest naturalistic explanation and does not claim deductive exclusion of supernatural causation.

charity.alternative: The particular coincidences may feel coordinated and personally salient rather than merely generic.
charity.decisiveQualification: Personal salience does not itself establish low population-level probability or supernatural selection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The population, cultural-script, and coincidence mechanism coherently undercuts inference from selected events to supernatural causation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explanation invokes credible general mechanisms but supplies no quantitative base rates or detailed fit to each named event.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly develops the central coincidence-naturalism bridge and addresses the section's principal explanatory clash.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy recognizes the story as appealing while preserving the decisive distinction between perceived coordination and comparative probability.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names the culturally familiar conversion script and ordinary coincidences as a naturalistic explanation for apparently coordinated stories.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Even the strongest arguments on both sides fail to compel a unique verdict, leaving both theistic and atheistic positions rationally permissible.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly says Bignon has characterized his view accurately and immediately states his assessment of the aggregate arguments on both sides.

components.text: Whether the aggregate comparative arguments rationally compel a uniquely Christian conclusion rather than permit continued reasonable disagreement.

response.rationale: Oppy accepts the stated characterization and directly addresses the force of the accumulated arguments, denying compulsion while allowing rational positions on both sides.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the question of compulsory force, although it does not separately assess the detailed coincidence comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clearly limited to whether the best aggregate arguments compel a particular position.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion is restrained to noncompulsion and explicitly permits rational disagreement rather than alleging decisive refutation.

charity.alternative: Arguments may rationally support Christianity without compelling every rational observer.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy's claim concerns noncompulsion, not the impossibility of personal rational justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between rational permissibility and compelled convergence is clear and internally consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion is asserted as an assessment of the best arguments without substantive comparison in this short span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally addresses independent balance and the epistemic standard governing the cumulative case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the important distinction between permissibility and compulsion and therefore avoids overstating its skeptical conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says that adding the best arguments on both sides does not compel arrival at one particular position.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: The converging improbabilities in Bignon's conversion story are well explained as providential acts intended by God to bring him to Christian faith.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly hands the conversation to Guillaume, who then narrates his conversion events continuously in the first person.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the central providential explanation by connecting several converging events with an asserted divine purpose of bringing Bignon to faith.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly supplies the proposed explanatory hypothesis but compresses its comparative defense.

precisionFindings.rationale: The providential hypothesis, intended purpose, and personal justificatory scope are all expressly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bignon frames this as what he thinks explains the events well, though the confidence modestly exceeds the supplied comparative warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Providential intention would explain convergence, but the bridge from unusual events to that intention remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The narrative supplies examples and personal fit but does not defend independence, improbability, or superiority over selection effects.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the providential-pattern explanation required by a central pro bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: This selected constructive span states the providential case without materially assessing a developed alternative explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls the events improbabilities and interprets them as God providentially controlling circumstances to bring him to faith.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Bignon's experiences need not compel an atheist in order to make his Christian conversion intellectually sensible and his resulting belief rationally permissible and personally justified.
moves.attributionBasis: Guillaume answers the host in the first person, describes the aims of his book, and explicitly addresses what Graham may reasonably grant.

components.text: Whether failure to compel atheists defeats the more modest claim that Christian belief can be rationally permissible and personally justified.

response.rationale: Bignon directly accepts noncompulsion and identifies personal justification and rational permissibility as the relevant, deliberately more modest target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive standard and cleanly distinguishes personal justification from proving atheism irrational.

precisionFindings.rationale: The personal and permissive scope is repeatedly stated and sharply separated from universal or coercive proof.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly disclaims the stronger million-dollar conclusion and claims only sensible, permissible personal belief.

charity.alternative: Oppy's noncompulsion thesis may still allow Christian belief to be rationally permissible.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon accepts precisely that limitation and treats permissibility, not universal convergence, as his successful burden.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from noncompulsion to a modest permissibility target is explicit, consistent, and resolves the apparent standard mismatch.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant rests on Oppy's conceded permissibility and Bignon's expressly limited aim, with only the underlying positive case left elsewhere.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximizes central-tier relevance by fixing the cumulative case's indispensable epistemic standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest skeptical position is accurately represented and incorporated rather than weakened or dismissed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly declines proving atheism irrational and embraces the concession that Christian belief may be justified, permissible, and sensible.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Persistent disagreement among expert philosophers of religion indicates that neither theistic nor atheistic arguments compel rational convergence, even after sustained inquiry.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Graham immediately before this passage, and the speaker discusses professional philosophers from Oppy's characteristic first-person skeptical position.

components.text: Whether sustained expert inquiry produces convergence sufficient to raise the case beyond rational permissibility to compelling public support.

response.rationale: Oppy reinforces the noncompulsion standard with persistent expert disagreement, while leaving Bignon's narrower personal-permissibility claim intact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the public-convergence issue but does not defeat, and only indirectly bears on, the narrower personal-justification claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim about nonconvergence among philosophers of religion is clear, though the evidential significance of disagreement is partly implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move uses disagreement as an indicator against super-compelling arguments, not as proof that every position is equally supported.

charity.alternative: Personal justification can remain even when equally informed experts do not converge.
charity.decisiveQualification: The disagreement evidence bears on compulsion and clear public superiority, not directly on all personal justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Persistent informed disagreement is relevant to claimed compellingness, though the move leaves possible non-evidential causes of disagreement unexamined.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence of prominent theists and atheists is concrete support, but no systematic account of expertise or disagreement causes is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central independent-balance bridge by challenging expected expert convergence.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy's stated conclusion respects the limited consequence of disagreement and does not infer wholesale irrationality.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt points to lifelong philosophers of religion divided between theism and atheism and denies hidden super-compelling arguments at higher expertise.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Naturalism has a structurally parallel cumulative case, while arguments from evil and divine hiddenness require theists to identify which premises they reject and accept the resulting commitments.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker refers to a case for naturalism developed in his own works and then explicitly describes theists as the opposing audience evaluating it.

components.text: Whether a modest cumulative Christian case must also reckon with a structurally parallel naturalist case and major counterarguments from evil and hiddenness.
Whether providential interpretation remains comparatively adequate after arguments from evil and divine hiddenness are included.

response.rationale: Oppy directly broadens the comparative ledger, identifying a parallel naturalist cumulative case and demanding premise-level responses to evil and hiddenness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the cumulative comparative burden and the providential challenge, though the selected span does not itself develop the full naturalist case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The structural comparison and the premise-rejection demand are clear, limited, and explicitly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity asserted is methodological: reflective theists must identify rejected premises and resulting commitments, a proportionate dialectical demand.

charity.alternative: Theists can reject premises in evil and hiddenness arguments without abandoning all providential explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy asks them to identify those premises and accept commitments rather than assuming the arguments automatically succeed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parallel-case structure and premise-rejection consequence are explicit and avoid inferring naturalism solely from the existence of objections.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Serious argument families are specifically identified, but their premises and the promised cumulative naturalist case are not developed here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by placing evil, hiddenness, and naturalist explanation into the total evidential comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats theistic replies as available and places a fair burden on their specification instead of caricaturing them.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names evil and divine hiddenness and expressly asks which premises theists reject and what commitments those rejections incur.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Christian providence need not imply that God tries maximally to convert everyone, because God may have morally sufficient reasons for saving some people and not others.
moves.attributionBasis: The first-person speaker identifies his Calvinist view and his own work on free will and divine providence, clearly marking Guillaume's response.

components.text: Whether selective providential intervention is inconsistent with God's not converting everyone or can be compatible with morally sufficient reasons.

response.rationale: Bignon directly addresses the selectivity aspect of hiddenness by denying that providence entails maximal efforts to convert all people and positing morally sufficient reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive consistency challenge but provides only the modal answer, not the promised account of the morally sufficient reasons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Calvinist consistency claim is clear, and the speaker expressly acknowledges that unresolved puzzles remain.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims consistency rather than likelihood and candidly acknowledges puzzles addressed outside the selected span.

charity.alternative: Uneven conversion opportunities may create a serious hiddenness and compassion problem for providence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon acknowledges that puzzle but maintains only that morally sufficient reasons could make selectivity consistent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility claim is logically possible, but morally sufficient reasons are asserted rather than specified, leaving a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No concrete moral reason or independent support is supplied for why salvation would be selectively distributed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely addresses the subsidiary selective-providence bridge and reaches the top of that tier despite underdevelopment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is recognized as a genuine puzzle, although its strongest moral pressure is not answered in detail.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly denies that God must try hardest to convert everyone, asserts morally sufficient reasons, and concedes remaining puzzles.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The cultural and historical diversity of religious experiences and their interpretations substantially weakens testimonial support for Christianity specifically.
moves.attributionBasis: The host asks Graham which concern matters, and the response develops Oppy's skeptical argument using culturally specific Australian religious testimony.

components.text: Whether selective providence can explain the culturally and historically uneven content of reported religious experiences without weakening Christian specificity.
Whether interpretation of personally salient experience remains distinctively Christian once cultural dependence is considered.

response.rationale: Oppy shifts from distribution of salvation to the directly related distribution and interpretation of experience, using cultural specificity as evidence against a uniquely Christian reading.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the wider selectivity problem and directly challenges experiential specificity, though it does not answer the proposed unspecified moral reasons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly about reduced testimonial evidential value after learning of culturally diverse interpretations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy argues that diversity makes evidential value difficult to see, stopping short of claiming that all religious testimony is worthless.

charity.alternative: Different cultures could encounter the same reality while interpreting it through local conceptual resources.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such mediation still weakens testimony for Christianity specifically unless an independent adjudicator favors that interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move validly distinguishes generic experiential occurrence from testimony supporting a culturally specific Christian conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete historical-cultural contrast supports the thesis, though broader representative documentation would strengthen it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly develops the central experiential-diversity bridge and strongly bears on specifically Christian support.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument allows experience while focusing fairly on the specificity problem created by divergent cultural interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites diverse interpretations and the absence of Jesus-specific testimony in pre-Christian Australian contexts as a cultural-dependence example.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Non-Christian religious experiences may count against naturalism without supporting Christianity, while unreliable practices can be rejected case by case without thereby discrediting Bignon's experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly invites Guillaume's answer, and the speaker cites Ken Pearce, agrees selectively with Oppy, and contrasts dubious practices with his own experience.

components.text: Whether diverse non-Christian experiences uniformly defeat Christianity or can instead count against naturalism while requiring case-specific theological assessment.

response.rationale: Bignon directly resists wholesale neutralization by distinguishing generic anti-naturalist force, mistaken interpretation, and unreliable practices on a case-by-case basis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive diversity issue but offers a framework for future differentiation more than a completed principled adjudication.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinctions are recoverable, but the criteria separating genuine experience, wrong interpretation, and unreliable practice remain under-specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move cautiously proposes possible differential treatment rather than claiming that rival experiences have already been exhaustively explained.

charity.alternative: Diverse incompatible experiences weaken testimony for Christianity specifically even if some oppose naturalism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon accepts the need for theological explanation and case-specific reliability assessment rather than treating all experiences as Christian evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The three-way distinction is coherent, but its application depends on undeveloped non-question-begging reliability criteria.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites a possible framework but supplies little representative evidence or defended warrant for classifying rival cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central experiential-diversity bridge and attempts the required rival adjudication.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly preserves the specificity problem, though it does not supply enough criteria to resolve it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says non-Christian experiences may undermine naturalism while requiring explanations for context, misinterpretation, or unreliable experience.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Preferring a Christian interpretation of religious experience is not special pleading if Christianity and Bignon's conversion possess stronger supporting reasons than rival claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The host directs the special-pleading question to Guillaume, whose first-person defense follows continuously before Graham begins a new challenge.

components.text: Whether preferring Christianity amid diverse incompatible experiences is arbitrary special pleading or justified by stronger comparative reasons.

response.rationale: Bignon directly states the condition under which special pleading would arise and denies that condition by claiming stronger reasons for Christianity and his interpretation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive arbitrariness charge, but the stronger comparative reasons are asserted rather than presented in this span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The special-pleading condition and comparative claim are clearly stated with stable scope and terminology.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim to better reasons is qualified as the speaker's assessment, but the selected evidence does not display those reasons.

charity.alternative: Christian preference would be special pleading if rival claims had equal support and were dismissed selectively.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon accepts that criterion and locates disagreement in the comparative evidential premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional analysis of special pleading is sound, but the premise that Christian reasons are stronger remains unsupported here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The decisive comparative superiority claim is largely asserted without examples or defended evaluation in the selected span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central experiential-diversity challenge by proposing comparative, rather than arbitrary, preference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest special-pleading formulation is accurately stated and answered at its decisive conditional premise.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines special pleading through equal reasons and claims that Christianity and Bignon's interpretation instead possess better reasons.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: When Christian and Muslim religious experiences appear comparable, historical and intellectual evidence concerning Muhammad, Jesus, and the resurrection can adjudicate between their incompatible interpretations.
moves.attributionBasis: The host asks Guillaume how to decide between equally compelling experiences, and Guillaume answers by proposing comparison of historical evidence.

components.text: How incompatible but apparently comparable Christian and Muslim experiences can be adjudicated without simply privileging one's own experience.

response.rationale: Bignon directly proposes an independent referee—comparative historical and intellectual evidence concerning Muhammad, Jesus, and the resurrection—when experience alone ties.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive adjudication demand and identifies a concrete replacement evidential domain.

precisionFindings.rationale: The experiential tie, proposed referee, and comparative conclusion are all clearly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bignon openly marks his Christian standpoint, but claims much stronger Christian evidence before presenting its detailed warrant.

charity.alternative: Christian and Muslim experiences may be experientially tied and mutually incompatible.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply grants the experiential tie and invokes genuinely independent historical and intellectual comparison rather than experience itself.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Independent evidence can coherently break an experiential tie, though the move does not yet demonstrate that the evidence favors Christianity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Relevant comparison topics are named, but the asserted superiority of Christian evidence is not substantiated within this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central rival-adjudication bridge at nearly maximal central-tier relevance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest rival-experience problem is accepted, and the proposed adjudicator directly preserves its legitimate demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt proposes comparison of sources about Muhammad and Jesus and the resurrection argument as intellectual referees when experience is tied.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Comparative assessment of Christianity and Islam requires substantial expertise, and the available historical record does not plainly establish a stronger case for Christianity.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Graham, who answers with first-person cautions about his expertise and then compares the historical records of Islam and Christianity.

components.text: Whether comparative historical evidence plainly favors Christianity over Islam strongly enough to adjudicate an experiential tie.

response.rationale: Oppy directly challenges the proposed referee by emphasizing the expertise required and the comparatively richer record for early Islam on some questions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive historical-superiority premise and supplies a specific countercomparison rather than generic skepticism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully limits its conclusion by noting that comparative strength depends on what is being authenticated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy acknowledges limited expertise and argues only that Christian historical superiority is difficult to establish plainly.

charity.alternative: Christian sources might be stronger for particular resurrection or reliability questions despite Islam's recency.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy expressly says the comparison depends on what one is trying to authenticate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply validly shows that a proposed historical referee requires question-specific comparison and cannot rest on a general superiority assertion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The relative recency and richer early Islamic cultural record are specific supports, though the full comparative historiography is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the central independent-balance bridge by attacking the proposed historical tiebreaker.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest issue-specific Christian possibility is preserved rather than displaced by a blanket documentary comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts knowledge of Islam immediately after Muhammad with Christianity's first 150 years and makes authentication question-dependent.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: The quality, quantity, and tested historical reliability of New Testament sources provide Christianity with stronger historical support than Islam after careful comparison.
moves.attributionBasis: Guillaume identifies his own limited expertise but then presents the Christian apologetic case, contrasting New Testament and Quranic source reliability.

components.text: Whether Christianity can claim a comparative historical advantage based on source quality, quantity, and tested reliability rather than mere confidence.

response.rationale: Bignon directly answers with named evidential dimensions—source quality, document count, geographical and naming accuracy, and scholarly testing—while conceding limited expertise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative demand with concrete criteria, although its appeal to unnamed experts leaves verification compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is clear, but quality and historical reliability cover multiple dimensions that are not sharply distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker concedes limited expertise, yet calls Christian evidence much superior on the basis of compressed and partly indirect support.

charity.alternative: Islam's recency may yield a stronger record for some historical or cultural questions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon shifts to particular source-quality and reliability criteria rather than denying the relevance of recency altogether.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed criteria are relevant, but accuracy on incidental details does not by itself establish the central supernatural or theological claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The superiority claim relies heavily on unnamed expert research and selective reliability indicators without direct comparative documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks independent balance through a concrete historical case, despite the warrant gaps.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response uses a legitimate comparative distinction, though it does not fully engage Oppy's question-dependent qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes source quality, document quantity, geographical and naming accuracy, and serious researchers to claim New Testament superiority.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Christianity's larger surviving documentary record partly reflects later institutional dominance and selective preservation, so document quantity alone is not compelling evidence of historical superiority.
moves.attributionBasis: Graham explicitly returns to an earlier caution and explains how copying, preservation, and destruction practices shaped the surviving documentary record.

components.text: Whether the larger quantity of Christian documents independently indicates historical superiority or partly reflects later preservation and institutional selection.

response.rationale: Oppy directly attacks the document-quantity component by explaining how Christian dominance encouraged copying of Christian texts and neglect or destruction of alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts and undercuts one decisive evidential component, while leaving source quality and incidental accuracy separately unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully limited to the argument from weight of documentation rather than all historical evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The institutional-selection mechanism proportionately supports the limited conclusion that quantity alone is not compelling.

charity.alternative: Numerous Christian documents may still be historically valuable and some may be independently reliable.
